APUSH Virtual Exhibit

Railroads in the Civil War1861 – 1865

Exhibit Overview

Welcome to the Exhibit

Welcome to my digital exhibit showcasing the huge role railroads played in the Civil War. This exhibit shows how military trains, logistical advantages, and infrastructure sabotage allowed the Union to be victorious in the Civil War, leading the way to modern industrial warfare.

Tab II

Historical Photo & Map Gallery

Cushing, Charles · Alamy · 1861
Exhibit Image 1

Federal Union Railroad Battery Car (1861)

Cushing, Charles. "A FEDERAL UNION RAILROAD BATTERY TANK-LIKE IRON CLAD CAR WITH ARTILLERY." Alamy, 1861.

This drawing shows how military trains changed during the Civil War. The Union would build iron-plated battery cars to defend supply trains from the Confederate soldiers, who would often use guerrilla tactics and cavalry ambushes. These cars were built with holes through which soldiers could shoot cannons and infantry weapons, turning them into moving fortresses. This technology foreshadowed the armored trains of the late-19th and early-20th century.

Bettmann · Bettmann Archive · 1864
Exhibit Image 2

Ruins of the Atlanta Rail Yard (1864)

Bettmann. "Ruins of the Atlanta Rail Yard." Bettman Archive, 1864.

This photograph shows the destruction of the train tracks in Atlanta, Georgia, after General Sherman's raid. Atlanta was an important place for the South during the war, connecting many of its major supply lines. Union forces completely decimated this engine house and mangled the rails to prevent the Confederates from sending reinforcements to their army. This picture is proof of the Union's tough strategy of targeting infrastructure to win the war.

American Rails · 1861
Exhibit Image 3

American Railroad Infrastructure Map (1861)

"Railroads During the Civil War." American Rails, 1861.

This map from the Civil War era shows the clear difference between railroad infrastructure in the North and the South. The north shows a dense, interconnected system of rails that bridged their agricultural centers and factories to their ports. In contrast, the rail systems in the south are sparse, not well-connected, and mainly designed to transport cotton. This illustrates why the Union had an upper hand in transporting soldiers and goods during the Civil War.

Primary Source Analysis
Pacific Railway Act, 1862

Wartime Statute Excerpt — Section 2
"SEC. 2. And be it further enacted, That the right of way through the public lands be, and the same is hereby, granted to said company for the construction of said railroad and telegraph line; and the right, power, and authority is hereby given to said company to take from the public lands adjacent to the line of said road, earth, stone, timber, and other materials for the construction thereof; said right of way is granted to said railroad to the extent of two hundred feet in width on each side of said railroad where it may pass over the public lands, including all necessary grounds for stations, buildings, workshops, and depots, machine shops, switches, side tracks, turntables, and, water stations. The United States shall extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles to all lands falling under the operation of this act and required for the said right of way and; grants hereinafter made."
Source: Pacific Railway Act, 1862
National Archives · Official Record

Summary

The Pacific Railway Act was signed into law by President Abraham Lincoln on July 1, 1862, and it allowed for the construction of the nation's first transcontinental railroad. The government tasked private companies in the Union Pacific to build tracks westward from Omaha and companies in the Central Pacific to build eastward from Sacramento. To fund this, the government gave companies a 400-foot right of way through public land with resource rights. However, they were also required to construct a military telegraph line. The companies were also provided 30-year government bonds—$16,000 per mile on flat land, $32,000 in the Great Basin, and $48,000 in the mountains—and were granted 10 alternate sections of land per mile of track. The act aimed to open the West to farming, mining, and settlement, while also shortening travel from New York to San Francisco from months to days, making transportation to Asian trade markets easier. Connecting California and Oregon to the rest of the nation encouraged these resource-rich states to remain loyal to the Union during the Civil War, while also providing an easy path for the government to quickly deploy troops and supplies.

Historical Context

The historical context of the Pacific Railway Act of 1862 was the secession of the Southern states. Through the 1850s, sectional debates occurred in Congress over where to build the transcontinental railroad, since both northern and southern politicians wanted the economic benefits that would come from having the railroad. However, when southern states seceded in 1860 and 1861, the Republican Party was left to pass several acts, including the Pacific Railway Act, for the benefit of the North.

Purpose

The main purpose of the Pacific Railway Act was to open the American West to industrial settlement. The act supported private companies with the financial aid of the federal government to ensure the success of the transcontinental railroad. It also incentivized companies to overcome geographic barriers like the Rocky Mountains quickly, since they would be granted more valuable bonds for doing so.

Key People
►
Herman Haupt: A competent Union Brigadier General and civil engineer. He created standardized bridge parts, allowing Union crews to rebuild destroyed railroad bridges in under a day.
►
Abraham Lincoln: The Union President during the Civil War who recognized the value of having an interconnected railway system early in the war. He used the telegraphs to quickly communicate with his generals, and he used the rail systems to transport important supplies. Lincoln also signed the Pacific Railway Act into law in 1862, expanding the railway system even more.
►
William Tecumseh Sherman: Famous Union General who was known for using total war tactics. He ordered the destruction of many of the Confederacy's railroad lines, cutting off their access to supplies and troops and making it easier to win the war.
Key Statistics
►
The Union had about 22,000 miles of railroad track, while the Confederacy had only about 9,000 miles (Burns "Civil War Railroads: Map and Facts (North vs South)").
►
In 1861, Northern factories produced 96% of the locomotives in the United States, leaving the South with barely any ability to replace broken or captured trains (Arrington "Industry and Economy during the Civil War").
►
The North had a standardized rail gauge of 4 feet, 8.5 inches (Rogers "Railroad Facts… Construction, Safety, and More"), allowing trains to run anywhere across the Union. In contrast, the South used over a dozen different rail gauges, making it hard to transport goods long distances and often forcing cargo transfers.
Key PEDLIGS
►
Baltimore and Ohio (B&O) Railroad: The main Northern railroad line and the primary supply route between Washington, D.C., and the Western parts of the war.
►
The Great Locomotive Chase (1862): A Union military raid in Georgia where Union spies hijacked The General, a Confederate locomotive, to destroy important Western & Atlantic railroad tracks.
►
Battle of Chickamauga Rail Deployment (1863): The Union moved 22,000 troops over 1,200 miles using railway systems in only 11 days to reinforce surrounded forces at Chattanooga, Tennessee ("Hamilton County and City of Chattanooga, TN"). It was the quickest army mobilization of the war.
►
United States Military Railroad (USMRR): Created by the Union, it was the largest railroad system in the world at the time, connecting thousands of miles of captured and built tracks.
►
Sherman's Bowties: The nickname of Confederate rail lines that Union soldiers heated over fires and bent around trees as a total war tactic, making the iron fully unrepairable and forcing Southern workers to rebuild broken tracks from scratch.
►
Confederate Iron Shortage: Without sufficient iron factories, such as the Tredegar Iron Works, the South frequently had to rip up minor rail lines to repair their more important, mainline tracks.

Educational FAQ

The North's advantage was mainly due to its large capacity to build railroads and its track unification. The Union had over double the total track mileage of the South and built almost all locomotives and rails that existed in the United States. Due to this, it was much easier for the Union to repair locomotives and replace tracks, maintaining a healthy flow of soldiers and supplies. The Union also had five times more skilled railroad workers than the Confederacy, making repairs fast and efficient. Additionally, the North had uniform railroad track parameters, allowing trains to transport items anywhere across the Union.
Railroads changed military medicine and care for soldiers by transporting new "hospital trains," which included suspended passenger beds to absorb the shocks from trains. These allowed the Union to quickly transport wounded soldiers out of harm's way to standard hospitals in cities while offering ample care on the way there. Hospital cars had tiers of bunks, kitchens, and medicine cabinets, and some even came with operating rooms for urgent injuries.
Telegraph lines were strung along railroad tracks, allowing President Lincoln and his generals to receive instant battle information and send military commands in real time. Commanders could order troops and supplies to arrive at certain locations simultaneously for coordinated military attacks. Furthermore, the constant contact that the telegraph provided allowed trains to be rerouted around damaged tracks or technical failures. The Union even created The US Military Telegraph Corps (USMTC) to manage the paths of trains using telegraphs.

Key Takeaway

The Civil War was the first major conflict where railroads played a decisive strategic role, forever changing how nations wage war and move armies across vast distances.
